title: Microsoft Fabric Data Governance Tutorial
summary: An independent tutorial-site walkthrough of Fabric's governance surface — the OneLake catalog's Explore/Govern/Secure tabs, a medallion-architecture governance-gate pattern, and a routine governance operating cadence — last verified June 2026.
audience: Fabric admins, domain owners, and platform teams operationalizing governance across workspaces rather than reading a feature-by-feature reference.
why_it_matters: Documents a navigation change (retirement of the standalone Purview Hub) and a routine operating cadence that are the kind of practical, time-sensitive detail Microsoft Learn's conceptual governance docs tend not to spell out.
takeaways: Fabric governance functionality is organized into three OneLake catalog tabs: Explore, Govern, and Secure, each with a different purpose and audience.
The standalone Purview Hub in Fabric's navigation was retired at the end of January 2026, with its insights moved into the Govern tab.
A medallion architecture can have governance gates attached to each layer (bronze/silver/gold) rather than governance being a single end-of-pipeline step.
Enabling OneLake data access roles (OneSecurity) on a Direct Lake-backed Lakehouse can force a semantic model to fall back to DirectQuery, per the post.
Govern-tab insights are refreshed daily from admin monitoring data, so it lags real time and should be read as trend data, not a live security console.

claims.text: As of the end of January 2026, the standalone Purview Hub previously present in the Fabric navigation was retired; security insights, sensitivity-label coverage, and DLP policy status that used to live there moved into the Govern tab of the OneLake catalog, per the post's citation of the Fabric blog announcement.

The OneLake catalog exposes three distinct governance-related tabs: an Explore tab for discovering items filtered by domain/type/sensitivity, a Govern tab surfacing health metrics like missing descriptions and endorsement/label coverage, and a Secure tab for reviewing user and group role assignments across workspaces.

Access control in Fabric layers across four distinct mechanisms: workspace-level RBAC roles via Entra ID groups, per-item permissions (ReadAll/ReadData/Build), OneLake security (OneSecurity) roles at folder/table/row/column granularity, and SQL-endpoint-level row-level security and column masking.

Enabling OneLake data access roles (OneSecurity) on a Lakehouse that backs a Direct Lake semantic model can cause that semantic model to fail Direct Lake mode and fall back to DirectQuery; the recommended workaround per the post is to manage row-level security at the semantic model layer instead until the incompatibility is resolved.

A practical medallion-architecture governance pattern applies different controls per layer: bronze restricted to engineering workspace roles with sensitivity labels at ingestion, silver adding schema validation and item-level consumer permissions plus OneSecurity row filters, and gold requiring catalog certification, domain-owner endorsement, tested row-level security, and a completed DLP scan before being marked discoverable.

Govern-tab insights are driven by an admin monitoring data refresh that runs on roughly a daily cadence, so they reflect the prior day's state rather than real time; the Secure tab is the better source for checking current, live permission assignments.

The Explore tab in the OneLake catalog only surfaces items the current user already has access to, so getting a full-estate discovery view requires either Fabric Admin rights or domain owners being granted read access across all workspaces in their domain.

A suggested governance operating cadence spans multiple frequencies: daily capacity and pipeline-failure checks, weekly work through Govern-tab recommended actions, monthly workspace access audits and stale-group cleanup, and quarterly archiving of stale Lakehouses alongside a domain ownership and storage-tier cost review.

Domain architecture is recommended to align to functional business units such as Finance or Supply Chain rather than mirroring org-chart structure, with workspaces used underneath each domain for team-level collaboration, and a practical guideline of keeping roughly 15-20 workspaces per domain to limit sprawl.
